title: Humans understand what AI cannot
author: Build Cognitive Resonance
summary: The essay explores 'understanding' from three angles -- pedagogical, philosophical, and personal -- arguing that AI's failures as a tutor are not incidental bugs but predictable consequences of what understanding actually requires. Drawing on a teacher's definition of understanding as 'knowledge of generalizations that can support procedural learning' and Dan Willingham's framing of understanding as 'remembering in disguise,' the author argues that large language models are 'completely useless' at the connective, schema-building work that constitutes real understanding because they lack any model of what's happening in a particular user's mind. The piece then turns to John Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment to establish philosophically that fluent symbol manipulation is not the same as understanding, before pairing that argument with Helen Keller's own account of her cognitive awakening at the well-house as lived evidence for Searle's abstract claim. The essay closes by contrasting AI's confident fluency with the human capacities Keller's story dramatizes: curiosity, social connection, and the capacity for a word to 'awaken a soul,' concluding that AI's absence of these things isn't a temporary technical gap but a categorical one.
points: Cites a teacher's working definition of understanding -- knowledge of explicit principles or generalizations that can guide activity -- to argue that procedural and conceptual knowledge must develop together, which is precisely what current AI tutors fail to replicate.

Uses Dan Willingham's framing of understanding as 'remembering in disguise' -- connecting new ideas to existing ones through active mental rearrangement -- to explain specifically why AI chatbots fail as tutors: they have no model of what a student already knows to connect to.

Deploys Searle's Chinese Room argument to establish that passing a Turing-style test for symbol manipulation is categorically different from understanding, then pairs it with Helen Keller's autobiographical account of her own cognitive awakening as lived proof of the same claim.

Frames Keller's breakthrough moment at the well-house -- when 'water' spelled into her hand stopped being imitation and became meaning -- as the clearest possible illustration of what AI cannot do: connect a symbol to a genuinely held concept.
quotes: Understanding is a Big Juicy Word, like justice or freedom, that is powerful and important yet perilous to define. No definition could possibly encompass the entirety of what we mean by understanding, yet we all have a general sense of it means.

It's knowledge of generalizations that can support procedural learning, and it's why procedural and conceptual knowledge have to happen in tandem. You can't first learn all the procedures and then learn the concepts later.

Dan Willingham describes understanding as remembering in disguise because it involves connecting new ideas to existing old ideas and then rearranging them -- making comparisons we hadn't made before, or thinking about a feature we previously ignored.
In contrast, large-language models at present are completely useless at this, in part because they lack any depth of understanding of what is happening in the minds of their users.
The program enables the person in the room to pass the Turing Test for understanding Chinese but he does not understand a word of Chinese.

As the cool stream gushed over one hand she spelled into the other the word water, first slowly, then rapidly. I stood still, my whole attention fixed upon the motions of her fingers. Suddenly I felt a misty consciousness as of something forgotten -- a thrill of returning thought; and somehow the mystery of language was revealed to me.
The living word awakened her soul -- what a beautiful testament to the power of human language to express human thought.
